weeks.lesson_plan_markdown:
# Week 8: Sewing Actions

## Overview
Week 8 turns fabric and tool vocabulary into process language. After Week 7, students can already talk about fabrics, texture, and material use. This week moves into simple sewing workflow: what action happens first, what tool is used, where the student sews, and how the process finishes.

The main written artifact stays A2-first. Students do not write a paragraph and do not work toward a base word count. Instead, they complete a scaffolded Simple Sewing Process Card with 6 required sentence-frame lines and 1 optional challenge sentence. This keeps the task concrete, reviewable, and aligned with early Module 1 writing guardrails.

## Learning Objectives
- Recognize and name common sewing-action words in English.
- Connect familiar studio tools to simple sewing actions.
- Read a short step-by-step hem process and answer clear sequence and detail questions.
- Listen to a short sewing sequence and identify the correct next step, tool, and final action.
- Use imperative process language such as `Cut the fabric`, `Fold the edge`, and `Check the stitches`.
- Use sequence words such as `first`, `then`, `next`, `after that`, and `finally`.
- Complete a scaffolded process card with 6 required lines and 1 optional challenge line.
- Explain one simple sewing process orally in 5 to 6 short supported steps during the teacher session.

## Professional Fashion-Design Context
Week 8 connects English to introductory sewing workflow, early garment construction, and beginner studio instructions. Fashion Design students need this language when they follow a demonstration, prepare fabric, describe a sewing sample, or explain how they completed a simple classroom task such as marking, cutting, folding, pinning, sewing, and pressing.

The week also prepares students for later work on patternmaking, prototyping, and more detailed process writing. The focus should stay concrete and observable: what the student does, what tool they use, what part of the fabric they work on, and how they check the result.

## Language Objectives
- Name core sewing verbs such as `cut`, `fold`, `pin`, `sew`, `press`, `measure`, `mark`, and `check`.
- Recognize support verbs such as `trace`, `align`, `hold`, `place`, and `remove`.
- Name sewing objects such as `seam`, `stitch`, `hem`, `edge`, `thread`, `needle`, `line`, `scissors`, `pins`, `sewing machine`, `iron`, and `measuring tape`.
- Use sequence words such as `first`, `then`, `next`, `after that`, and `finally`.
- Use location and direction phrases such as `along the line`, `on the edge`, `at the hem`, `on the right side`, and `on the wrong side`.
- Use process-quality support words such as `straight`, `even`, `careful`, and `correct`.

## Materials Needed
- One Week 8 sewing workspace opener board with visible keys.
- One sewing-actions vocabulary board labeled with visible keys `A` to `J`.
- One tools-and-actions board for controlled tool phrase practice.
- One simple hem reading sequence board labeled with visible keys `A` to `F`.
- One reusable sewing-process gallery labeled `image A`, `image B`, `image C`, `image D`, and `image E`.
- One short listening audio clip or teacher read-aloud fallback for the listening task.
- Visible sentence frames for Week 8 process language.
- Student writing space for the Simple Sewing Process Card.
- Optional classroom support: scissors, measuring tape, pins, a sample seam or hem, and fabric pieces for live demonstration.

## Suggested Sequence
1. `m01w08-a01` Welcome Back: students bridge from Week 7 fabric and tool language into Week 8 sewing actions with one compact opener board.
2. `m01w08-a02` Sewing Action Vocabulary: students complete the main sewing-actions matching set, then use a short Portuguese bridge and one support sentence after the core matching.
3. `m01w08-a03` Tools + Actions: students complete controlled `Use ___ to ___` fill-blank phrases linked to the tools board.
4. `m01w08-a04` Read: students read a short hem process, use the keyed step board, and answer first-step, next-step, tool, and detail questions.
5. `m01w08-a05` Listen: students hear one short sewing sequence and answer explicit first, next, final, tool, and detail questions using the shared `image A` to `image E` process gallery.
6. `m01w08-a06` Phrase Practice: students complete fill-blank frames using sequence words, imperative action phrases, and `check ___`.
7. `m01w08-a07` Simple Sewing Process Card: students choose one simple process path from the shared gallery and complete a teacher-reviewed structured writing card.
8. `m01w08-a08` Review and Improve: students correct two short Week 8 process sentences and save the improved versions.
9. `m01w08-a09` Teacher Session: students practice pronunciation and explain one simple sewing process in short supported steps.

## Timing Estimate
- `m01w08-a01` 6 minutes
- `m01w08-a02` 14 minutes
- `m01w08-a03` 10 minutes
- `m01w08-a04` 12 minutes
- `m01w08-a05` 12 minutes
- `m01w08-a06` 10 minutes
- `m01w08-a07` 18 minutes
- `m01w08-a08` 7 minutes
- `m01w08-a09` 50 minutes

Total planned time: 139 minutes.

The asynchronous or app-style portion is 89 minutes. The teacher-led speaking session is 50 minutes.

## Differentiation Options
- Keep the process boards and galleries visible during reading, listening, writing, and speaking.
- Reduce the active production verbs to `cut`, `fold`, `pin`, `sew`, `press`, and `check` for learners who need more support.
- Let students choose the simpler hem process path rather than the stitch-sample path for the writing card.
- Provide a reduced word bank for the writing card if students need more support with tool phrases or sequence words.
- Let students point to the gallery while speaking in the teacher session.

## Extension Options
- Ask stronger learners to add the optional challenge sentence with a clear process reason.
- Invite stronger learners to add one extra quality sentence in speaking such as `The line should be straight and even.`
- In the teacher session, ask one short follow-up question about tool choice, safety, or why the final check matters.

## Notes for Future App Implementation
Week 8 should stay tightly aligned across image keys, process steps, and listening answers in a future app. The app-facing flow should preserve:

- one opener board for fast bridge and preview work
- one main sewing-actions matching set as the primary saved vocabulary output
- one controlled `Use ___ to ___` fill-blank task where the primary saved output stays phrase completion
- one reading task with a fixed visible-key strategy `A` to `F`
- one listening task whose audio script matches the shared process gallery and answer key exactly
- one fill-blank phrase-practice task where the primary saved output stays sentence completion
- one teacher-reviewed structured writing card with separate sentence-frame fields instead of a paragraph box
- one teacher-observed speaking checkpoint that shows the process gallery and frames but does not record audio

The Week 8 reusable process gallery should stay consistent across listening, writing, and speaking, and should use the same process path and visible image keys across those tasks.
weeks.teacher_notes_markdown:
# Teacher Notes: Week 8 - Sewing Actions

## Common Learner Difficulties
Students may confuse tool words with action words, especially `pins` versus `pin`, `iron` versus `press`, and `line` as a drawn line versus thread. They may also forget `to` in `Use ___ to ___`, leave out articles in phrases such as `fold the edge`, or lose the sequence order when they try to produce several steps at once. Another common difficulty is writing a list of words instead of complete imperative sentences.

## Classroom Management Suggestions
Keep the Week 8 process boards visible throughout the week. Students should be able to point to a step while they answer. Move steadily from recognition to production: opener, action matching, tool phrases, reading, listening, phrase practice, structured writing, correction, then speaking. During the writing task, encourage students to complete one line at a time instead of trying to write a paragraph or tell the whole process from memory.

## Professional Context Notes
Keep the week connected to beginner sewing workflow, small classroom samples, and clear studio actions. Students are not doing advanced garment-construction explanation yet. They are learning how to say what happens first, what tool is used, where the action happens, and how to check the result. This language is useful later for patternmaking, prototyping, simple tutorials, and technical-process description.

## Cultural or Industry Notes
Some learners may already know Portuguese sewing vocabulary very well but may not have clear English equivalents for simple classroom instructions. Keep the English target practical and high-frequency. Also explain that `right side` and `wrong side` refer to the sides of the fabric, not to moral ideas of right and wrong.

## Simplify This Week
Keep the writing card at exactly six required lines:
- `First, ___.`
- `Then, ___.`
- `Next, ___.`
- `After that, ___.`
- `Use ___ to ___.`
- `Finally, check ___.`

Use the shared `image A` to `image E` gallery as a visual reference, not as a scored choice. Accept one optional challenge sentence only if the student is ready: `This step is important because ___.` Mark the writing card by checking the 6 required lines, the sequence order, the tool phrase, and the final check line. In the speaking task, accept 5 short spoken steps with strong teacher prompting if needed.

## Extend This Week
Ask stronger learners to add the optional challenge sentence with a clear process reason. During the teacher session, invite one follow-up sentence about quality such as `The line should be straight` or about tool choice such as `Use an iron to press the hem.`

## Asynchronous or App-Based Adaptation
The opener, sewing-actions matching, tool-action phrase practice, reading task, listening task, phrase-practice task, and correction task can all be app-checked with immediate feedback. The Simple Sewing Process Card should remain teacher-visible because it is the main written artifact, uses 6 required lines plus 1 optional challenge sentence, and benefits from a small revision cycle. The speaking checkpoint should remain teacher-observed and non-recorded, with the app serving only to display the shared process gallery, sentence frames, and completion notes.

weeks.lesson_plan_markdown:
# Week 9: Introduction to Patternmaking English

## Overview
Week 9 turns Week 8 process language into introductory patternmaking English. Students already know how to talk about measuring, marking, and checking in a simple sewing sequence. This week they apply that process language to pattern pieces, body and garment measurements, and visible pattern markings such as grainline, fold line, seam allowance, notch, and dart.

The main written artifact stays A2-first. Students do not write a paragraph and do not work toward a base word count. Instead, they complete a scaffolded Basic Pattern Piece Description Card with 6 required sentence-frame lines and 1 optional challenge sentence. This keeps the writing concrete, teacher-reviewable, and aligned with early Module 1 guardrails.

## Learning Objectives
- Recognize and name common patternmaking tools, pattern pieces, and markings in English.
- Match measurement and pattern-mark vocabulary to clear visual references.
- Read a short patternmaking procedure and answer sequence and detail questions.
- Listen to a short pattern-piece instruction sequence and identify the correct image key, measurement, marking, and final label.
- Use short sentence frames such as `This is a sleeve pattern piece` and `This piece is for a skirt`.
- Use imperative language such as `Measure the waist`, `Mark the grainline`, `Trace the pattern piece`, and `Check the measurement`.
- Complete a scaffolded Basic Pattern Piece Description Card with 6 required lines and 1 optional challenge line.
- Explain one pattern piece orally in 5 to 6 short supported sentences during the teacher session.

## Professional Fashion-Design Context
Week 9 connects English to beginner patternmaking, garment-construction preparation, and visual reading of pattern diagrams. Fashion Design students need this language when they identify a pattern piece, follow a demonstration, label a basic shape, or explain what the piece is for.

The week also prepares students for later work on sketch description, construction planning, prototyping, and technical explanation. The focus should stay concrete and visible: what the piece is called, what garment it helps make, what measurement or marking appears on it, and what action happens first, next, and finally.

## Language Objectives
- Name patternmaking basics such as `patternmaking`, `pattern`, `pattern piece`, `pattern paper`, `block`, and `template`.
- Name specific pieces such as `front bodice`, `back bodice`, `sleeve`, `skirt front`, `skirt back`, `waistband`, `collar`, and `pocket`.
- Name measurements such as `bust`, `waist`, `hip`, `shoulder`, `armhole`, `sleeve length`, and `garment length`.
- Name pattern markings such as `grainline`, `fold line`, `seam allowance`, `notch`, `dart`, `center front`, `center back`, and `side seam`.
- Use process verbs such as `measure`, `mark`, `trace`, `label`, `check`, and `adjust`.
- Use location phrases such as `on the fold`, `along the line`, `at the center front`, and `at the side seam`.

## Materials Needed
- One Week 9 patternmaking workspace opener board with visible keys.
- One pattern-pieces-and-tools board labeled with visible keys `A` to `J`.
- One measurements-and-marks board labeled with visible keys `A` to `J`.
- One reading sequence board labeled with visible keys `A` to `F`.
- One reusable pattern-piece gallery labeled `image A`, `image B`, `image C`, `image D`, and `image E`.
- One short listening audio clip or teacher read-aloud fallback for the listening task.
- Visible sentence frames for Week 9 patternmaking language.
- Student writing space for the Basic Pattern Piece Description Card.
- Optional classroom support: paper pattern examples, a measuring tape, a ruler, a French curve, and printed pattern-piece cards.

## Suggested Sequence
1. `m01w09-a01` Welcome Back: students bridge from Week 8 sewing process language into Week 9 patternmaking language with one compact opener board.
2. `m01w09-a02` Patternmaking Vocabulary: students complete the main pattern-pieces-and-tools matching set, then use a short Portuguese bridge and one support sentence after the core matching.
3. `m01w09-a03` Measurements and Pattern Marks: students complete the main measurement-and-mark matching set using one clear keyed board.
4. `m01w09-a04` Read: students read a short patternmaking procedure, use the keyed sequence board, and answer first-step, next-step, marking, and detail questions.
5. `m01w09-a05` Listen: students hear one short pattern-piece instruction sequence and answer explicit image-key, measurement, marking, and label questions using the shared `image A` to `image E` gallery.
6. `m01w09-a06` Phrase Practice: students complete fill-blank frames using patternmaking imperatives and short purpose phrases.
7. `m01w09-a07` Basic Pattern Piece Description Card: students choose one simple pattern piece from the shared gallery and complete a teacher-reviewed structured writing card.
8. `m01w09-a08` Review and Improve: students correct two short Week 9 patternmaking sentences and save the improved versions.
9. `m01w09-a09` Teacher Session: students practice pronunciation and explain one pattern piece in short supported sentences.

## Timing Estimate
- `m01w09-a01` 6 minutes
- `m01w09-a02` 14 minutes
- `m01w09-a03` 14 minutes
- `m01w09-a04` 12 minutes
- `m01w09-a05` 12 minutes
- `m01w09-a06` 10 minutes
- `m01w09-a07` 18 minutes
- `m01w09-a08` 7 minutes
- `m01w09-a09` 50 minutes

Total planned time: 143 minutes.

The asynchronous or app-style portion is 93 minutes. The teacher-led speaking session is 50 minutes.

## Differentiation Options
- Keep the keyed boards and the reusable gallery visible during reading, listening, writing, and speaking.
- Reduce the active target language to `pattern piece`, `waist`, `grainline`, `measure`, `mark`, `trace`, `label`, and `check` for learners who need more support.
- Let students choose the simplest piece from the gallery for the writing card, such as `skirt front` or `pocket`.
- Provide a reduced word bank for the writing card if students need more support with markings or location phrases.
- Let students point to the visible pattern-piece image while speaking in the teacher session.

## Extension Options
- Ask stronger learners to add the optional challenge sentence with a clear reason such as why the grainline or notch matters.
- Invite stronger learners to add one extra location sentence in speaking such as `The notch is at the side seam.`
- In the teacher session, ask one short follow-up question about why a marking matters or what garment the piece belongs to.

## Notes for Future App Implementation
Week 9 should stay tightly aligned across image keys, pattern markings, and listening answers in a future app. The app-facing flow should preserve:

- one opener board for a fast bridge from sewing to patternmaking
- one main pattern-pieces-and-tools matching set as the primary saved vocabulary output
- one main measurements-and-marks matching set as a second primary visual-vocabulary output
- one reading task with a fixed visible-key strategy `A` to `F`
- one listening task whose audio script matches the shared pattern-piece gallery and answer key exactly
- one fill-blank phrase-practice task where the primary saved output stays sentence completion
- one teacher-reviewed structured writing card with separate sentence-frame fields instead of a paragraph box
- one teacher-observed speaking checkpoint that shows the pattern-piece gallery and frames but does not record audio

The Week 9 reusable pattern-piece gallery should stay consistent across listening, writing, and speaking, and should use the same visible image keys across those tasks.
weeks.teacher_notes_markdown:
# Teacher Notes: Week 9 - Introduction to Patternmaking English

## Common Learner Difficulties
Students may confuse `pattern` with `pattern piece`, or use a garment word when they need a piece name such as `sleeve pattern piece`. They may also mix up `waist` and `hip`, or confuse a body measurement with a pattern marking. Another common difficulty is leaving out articles in phrases such as `Mark the grainline` or dropping the fixed phrase `on the fold`. In writing, students may try to list vocabulary words instead of completing the sentence-frame lines.

## Classroom Management Suggestions
Keep the Week 9 keyed boards visible throughout the week. Students should be able to point to a marking or a piece while they answer. Move steadily from recognition to production: opener, pattern-piece matching, measurement-and-mark matching, reading, listening, phrase practice, structured writing, correction, then speaking. During the writing task, encourage students to complete one line at a time instead of trying to explain the whole pattern piece from memory.

## Professional Context Notes
Keep the week connected to beginner patternmaking, paper pattern use, measurement checking, and simple garment-construction preparation. Students are not doing advanced drafting explanation yet. They are learning how to say what a piece is called, what garment it belongs to, what marking appears on it, and what simple actions they take to prepare it.

## Cultural or Industry Notes
Many learners may already know strong Portuguese vocabulary for modelagem and garment parts, but the English equivalents may not feel stable yet. Keep the English target practical and high-frequency. Also explain that `block` is a basic starting pattern, but it should stay a light support word this week rather than the main production target.

## Simplify This Week
Keep the writing card at exactly six required lines:
- `This is a ___ pattern piece.`
- `This piece is for a ___.`
- `It has a ___ and a ___.`
- `First, ___.`
- `Then, ___.`
- `Finally, check ___.`

Use the shared `image A` to `image E` gallery as a visual reference, not as a scored choice during the writing task. Accept one optional challenge sentence only if the student is ready: `This piece is on the fold because ___.` Mark the writing card by checking the six required lines, the correct piece name, at least one accurate marking, one clear process action, and the final check line. In the speaking task, accept 5 short spoken sentences with strong teacher prompting if needed.

## Extend This Week
Ask stronger learners to add the optional challenge sentence with a clear reason. During the teacher session, invite one follow-up sentence about placement such as `The notch is at the side seam` or purpose such as `This piece helps make the front of the skirt.`

## Asynchronous or App-Based Adaptation
The opener, pattern-pieces matching, measurements-and-marks matching, reading task, listening task, phrase-practice task, and correction task can all be app-checked with immediate feedback. The Basic Pattern Piece Description Card should remain teacher-visible because it is the main written artifact, uses 6 required lines plus 1 optional challenge sentence, and benefits from a small revision cycle. The speaking checkpoint should remain teacher-observed and non-recorded, with the app serving only to display the shared pattern-piece gallery, sentence frames, and completion notes.

weeks.lesson_plan_markdown:
# Week 10: Describing a Sketch

## Overview
Week 10 is the first major integration week in Module 1. Students have already built vocabulary for garments, garment parts, figure and pose, color and silhouette, fabric and texture, sewing actions, and beginner patternmaking. This week they combine those pieces into one clear sketch description.

The main written artifact stays A2-first. Students do not write a paragraph and do not work toward a base word count. Instead, they complete a scaffolded Fashion Sketch Description Card with 6 required sentence-frame lines and 1 optional challenge sentence. This keeps the writing concrete, teacher-reviewable, and aligned with early Module 1 guardrails while still feeling like a milestone task.

## Learning Objectives
- Recognize and review integrated sketch-description vocabulary from earlier Module 1 weeks.
- Match English sketch-description words to Portuguese support and sort them into clear categories.
- Read three short sketch descriptions and match them to the correct keyed images.
- Listen to four numbered sketch descriptions and identify the correct image and visible details.
- Organize a simple sketch description from opening sentence to final design comment.
- Complete phrase frames such as `The figure is wearing ...`, `The garment has ...`, `The color palette is ...`, and `I chose ... because ...`.
- Complete a scaffolded Fashion Sketch Description Card with 6 required lines and 1 optional challenge line.
- Present one sketch orally in 5 to 6 short supported sentences during the teacher session.

## Professional Fashion-Design Context
Week 10 connects English to the kind of basic visual explanation Fashion Design students need when they talk about a croquis, explain a class sketch, or prepare a simple portfolio-style caption. The focus is not advanced critique. Students are learning how to say what the figure is doing, what the outfit looks like, what details are visible, what fabric could fit the design, and what the overall look communicates.

This week also prepares students for later work on design details, feedback, inspiration, and mini design boards. The description order matters professionally: identify the sketch, describe the outfit, mention color and silhouette, add details and fabric, then close with a short design comment.

## Language Objectives
- Name figure and sketch words such as `sketch`, `croquis`, `figure`, `pose`, `front view`, and `side view`.
- Name garment words such as `dress`, `jacket`, `top`, `pants`, `skirt`, and `outfit`.
- Name visible details such as `sleeve`, `neckline`, `pocket`, `zipper`, `hem`, and `buttons`.
- Use design-description words such as `color palette`, `silhouette`, `neutral`, `bright`, `soft`, `straight`, `loose`, `fitted`, and `flared`.
- Use fabric and design-comment words such as `cotton`, `denim`, `lightweight`, `structured`, `flowy`, `main feature`, `overall look`, `comfortable`, `playful`, and `elegant`.
- Use short integrated frames such as `The figure is wearing ...`, `The garment has ...`, `The color palette is ...`, `The silhouette is ...`, `I imagine this garment in ...`, and `The overall look is ...`.

## Materials Needed
- One Week 10 opener sketch board with visible keys and one clearly readable fashion look.
- One reusable sketch gallery labeled `image A`, `image B`, and `image C` for reading, writing, and speaking.
- One listening sketch gallery labeled `image A`, `image B`, `image C`, and `image D`.
- One short Week 10 listening audio clip or teacher read-aloud fallback using the same `image A` to `image D` listening gallery.
- Visible sentence frames for Week 10 sketch-description language.
- Student writing space for the Fashion Sketch Description Card.
- Optional classroom support: printed gallery cards, a projector, color swatches, or teacher-selected sketch references.

## Suggested Sequence
1. `m01w10-a01` Welcome Back: students look at one keyed sketch board and answer five short review questions about garment, detail, palette, silhouette, and possible fabric.
2. `m01w10-a02` Sketch Description Vocabulary Review: students complete one main English-Portuguese matching and category-sorting set for integrated Week 10 vocabulary.
3. `m01w10-a03` Read: students use the `image A` to `image C` gallery, read three short descriptions, and answer image-match and detail questions.
4. `m01w10-a04` Listen: students use the `image A` to `image D` gallery, listen to one numbered audio clip, and answer image and detail questions that match the script exactly.
5. `m01w10-a05` Organize the Description: students put six description sentences in logical order and complete two short support checks.
6. `m01w10-a06` Phrase Practice: students complete six fill-blank phrase frames for sketch, garment, color, silhouette, fabric, and design comment language.
7. `m01w10-a07` Fashion Sketch Description Card: students choose one sketch from the shared reading gallery and complete a teacher-reviewed structured writing card.
8. `m01w10-a08` Review and Improve: students correct two short Week 10 sketch-description sentences and save the improved versions.
9. `m01w10-a09` Teacher Session: students practice pronunciation and present one sketch in 5 to 6 short supported sentences.

## Timing Estimate
- `m01w10-a01` 6 minutes
- `m01w10-a02` 14 minutes
- `m01w10-a03` 12 minutes
- `m01w10-a04` 12 minutes
- `m01w10-a05` 10 minutes
- `m01w10-a06` 10 minutes
- `m01w10-a07` 20 minutes
- `m01w10-a08` 9 minutes
- `m01w10-a09` 50 minutes

Total planned time: 143 minutes.

The asynchronous or app-style portion is 93 minutes. The teacher-led speaking session is 50 minutes.

## Differentiation Options
- Keep the reading gallery and the listening gallery visible while students answer.
- Reduce the active target language to `sketch`, `figure`, `jacket`, `dress`, `color palette`, `silhouette`, `cotton`, and `overall look` for learners who need more support.
- Let students choose the simplest reading-gallery sketch for the writing card, such as the soft dress or denim jacket look.
- Provide a reduced word bank for the writing card if students need support with design-comment or fabric phrases.
- Let students point to visible sketch details while speaking in the teacher session.

## Extension Options
- Ask stronger learners to add the optional challenge sentence with one simple reason, such as `I chose denim because it looks strong and practical.`
- Invite stronger learners to add one extra line about inspiration or one additional visible detail after the main speaking frame.
- In the teacher session, ask one short follow-up question such as `Why did you choose this fabric?` or `What is the main feature?`

## Notes for Future App Implementation
Week 10 should preserve one stable interaction flow from recognition to production:

- one opener sketch board for a fast integration review
- one main vocabulary matching and sorting set as the primary saved vocabulary output
- one reading task with a fixed visible-key strategy `image A` to `image C`
- one listening task whose audio script matches the `image A` to `image D` listening gallery and answer key exactly
- one sentence-order task where the main saved output stays ordering
- one fill-blank phrase-practice task where the primary saved output stays sentence completion
- one teacher-reviewed structured writing card with separate sentence-frame fields instead of a paragraph box
- one teacher-observed speaking checkpoint that shows the selected sketch and speaking frames but does not record audio

The reading gallery should stay consistent across reading, writing, and speaking so students do not have to relearn a new set of images when they move into the main written and spoken artifacts.
weeks.teacher_notes_markdown:
# Teacher Notes: Week 10 - Describing a Sketch

## Common Learner Difficulties
Students may know the vocabulary in isolation but struggle to combine it into one clear description. Common problems include using `using` instead of `is wearing`, writing noun lists instead of complete sentences, mixing up `color palette` and `silhouette`, and transferring Portuguese adjective order into English phrases such as `jacket denim short` instead of `short denim jacket`. Some learners may also forget plural details such as `buttons` and `pockets`, or use `because` without a full reason clause.

## Classroom Management Suggestions
Keep the reading gallery and the listening gallery visible throughout the week. Students should be able to point to the sketch while they answer. Move steadily from recognition to production: opener, vocabulary review, reading, listening, ordering, phrase practice, structured writing, correction, then speaking. During the writing task, remind students to complete one line at a time instead of trying to produce a paragraph from memory.

## Professional Context Notes
Keep the week connected to sketch presentation, beginner portfolio caption language, and short classroom explanation of a design look. Students are not doing advanced critique yet. They are learning how to explain what the figure is wearing, what colors and silhouette are visible, what details stand out, what fabric could fit the look, and what the overall design impression is.

## Cultural or Industry Notes
Many learners may already have strong Portuguese vocabulary for sketch, silhouette, palette, and fabric categories, but the English phrases may still feel unstable. Keep the target language practical and repeated. Also explain that Fashion Design sketch descriptions often move from general impression to specific details, which is why the organization task matters this week.

## Simplify This Week
Keep the writing card at exactly six required lines:
- `This sketch shows a figure in ___.`
- `The figure is wearing ___.`
- `The garment has ___.`
- `The color palette is ___.`
- `The silhouette is ___.`
- `I imagine this garment in ___.`

Use the shared `image A` to `image C` gallery as a visible reference and have the student save one selected sketch key before writing. Accept one optional challenge line only if the student is ready: `I chose this sketch because ___.` Mark the writing card by checking the saved sketch reference, the six required lines, visible sketch alignment, complete sentence use, one clear garment detail, one clear color-palette line, one clear silhouette line, and one simple fabric idea. In the speaking task, accept 5 short spoken sentences with strong teacher prompting if needed.

## Extend This Week
Ask stronger learners to add the optional challenge line with one design reason. During the teacher session, invite one follow-up sentence about inspiration, comfort, or function, such as `I chose this fabric because it looks comfortable.` or `The design feels playful and modern.`

## Asynchronous or App-Based Adaptation
The opener, vocabulary review, reading task, listening task, ordering task, phrase-practice task, and correction task can all be app-checked with immediate feedback. The Fashion Sketch Description Card should remain teacher-visible because it is the main written artifact, uses 6 required lines plus 1 optional challenge sentence, and benefits from a small revision cycle. The speaking checkpoint should remain teacher-observed and non-recorded, with the app serving only to display the shared gallery, sentence frames, and completion notes.

assets.title: Week 11 opener board with one full look and three close-up detail crops
assets.description: A single board that shows one adult fashion garment or sketch in full view plus three close-up crops so students can move from overall observation to design-detail noticing.
assets.notes: Keep the full look and the three close-up crops visible together. Use stable literal keys that match the activity prompts. Avoid clutter, logos, or tiny unreadable labels.

assets.title: Week 11 keyed close-up vocabulary board A to J
assets.description: A clear adult-learning board with ten close-up garment details labeled A to J for explicit image-to-word matching.
assets.notes: Show closures, pockets, decorative details, and construction details clearly enough for mobile viewing. Keep the keys literal and visible. Do not add extra instructional text inside the image.

assets.title: Week 11 scavenger garment with point labels A to H
assets.description: One garment or sketch with eight unambiguous point labels so students can identify visible details and then classify some of them as functional, decorative, or both.
assets.notes: Point labels A to H must be large, clear, and placed exactly on the intended details. Preserve the same point strings in activity answer data and prompt notes.

assets.title: Week 11 reusable detail gallery image A to image D
assets.description: A reusable four-image detail gallery for reading, listening, writing, and speaking. Each gallery image should show one clearly identifiable garment detail with a stable visible key.
assets.notes: Keep image A to image D literal and stable. Use one zipper detail, one embroidery detail, one patch-pocket detail, and one ruffle detail so the reading, listening, writing, and speaking tasks can align tightly.

assets.title: Week 11 numbered detail-identification listening clip
assets.description: One short A2 listening clip with numbered descriptions aligned exactly to the Week 11 reusable detail gallery.
assets.notes: Keep the listening script only in audio_prompts.json. Do not create a separate transcript asset. The gallery labels, numbered script, question labels, options, and correct answers must match exactly.

image_prompts.purpose: Week 11 opener board for moving from one full garment view to close observation of design details.
image_prompts.visual_description: One adult-oriented fashion-design board with one full garment or fashion sketch in the main panel plus three close-up detail crops that clearly show a front zipper, a patch pocket, and a soft ruffle hem.
image_prompts.style_instructions: Use a clean fashion-sketch or fashion-education illustration style with adult proportions, strong contrast, and clear garment details suitable for an ESP fashion-design course.
image_prompts.composition_notes: Keep the full look and the three close-up crops visible together on one simple board. The image must be easy to scan on a phone screen and should support the opener questions without extra clutter.
image_prompts.text_in_image: Only minimal visible keys if needed for the opener questions.
image_prompts.avoid: Avoid brand logos, childlike styling, tiny unreadable labels, busy backgrounds, unrealistic construction details, and unrelated classroom objects.

weeks.lesson_plan_markdown:
# Week 11: Design Details

## Overview
Week 11 shifts from full sketch description to close observation of garment details. Students learn to notice and name visible details, say where they are placed, and explain whether they are functional, decorative, or both. The week ends with one scaffolded detail-caption card and one short teacher-supported speaking explanation.

## Learning Objectives
- Identify common garment design details such as closures, pockets, decorative features, and visible construction details.
- Use short sentence frames to say where a detail is and what it does.
- Distinguish between functional and decorative roles in simple English.
- Read and listen to short detail captions tied to stable image keys.
- Produce one structured design-detail caption card with six required short lines.

## Professional Fashion-Design Context
Students use the kind of English they need for early critique, sketch annotation, sewing and patternmaking observation, and short portfolio-caption writing. The focus on details supports later design explanation, feedback, and mini design-board work.

## Language Objectives
- Name details such as zipper, patch pocket, embroidery, and ruffle.
- Use location phrases such as on the front, near the neckline, and at the side.
- Use There is and There are for visible details.
- Use frames such as It is functional because ..., It is decorative because ..., It adds ..., and It makes ....

## Materials Needed
- Week 11 opener board with one full look and three close-up detail crops.
- Week 11 keyed vocabulary board A to J.
- Week 11 scavenger garment with point labels A to H.
- Week 11 reusable detail gallery image A to image D.
- Week 11 listening clip aligned to the reusable gallery.
- Optional projected or printed copies of the reusable gallery for the writing and speaking tasks.

## Suggested Sequence
1. Start with the opener so students move from one full look to close-up detail noticing.
2. Teach the core vocabulary through the keyed close-up board.
3. Use the scavenger garment to connect visible points to detail names and simple role language.
4. Model short captions through reading before the listening task.
5. Use the listening task with the same stable gallery to reinforce the same details.
6. Consolidate the language with short phrase-practice fill blanks.
7. Move into the main structured writing card with one chosen gallery image.
8. End the online sequence with two narrow correction cards.
9. Use the teacher session for pronunciation support and one short spoken explanation.

## Timing Estimate
The student-facing weekly flow is designed for about 141 minutes total, including a 50-minute teacher-observed speaking session.

## Differentiation Options
- Keep Portuguese instructions visible while students produce English answers.
- Pre-teach only four core detail words first for learners who need more support.
- Let stronger students use the optional challenge line in the writing card.
- During the speaking task, allow students to read from the saved caption card before speaking more freely.

## Extension Options
- Ask students to compare two details from the gallery using simple contrast language.
- Ask students to add one extra sentence with It makes the garment look ....
- Reuse the gallery for a short warm-up in Week 12 or Week 13.

## Notes for Future App Implementation
The app should keep stable visible keys on the screen whenever a task depends on them. The writing card should save the chosen image key plus each required line separately. The listening task should allow replay and reveal the script only after the first completed attempt. The teacher review flow should show the selected image key, the saved structured lines, a short checklist, common error prompts, and a return-for-revision option for the writing task only.
weeks.teacher_notes_markdown:
# Teacher Notes: Week 11 — Design Details

## Common Learner Difficulties
- Students may confuse the name of the detail with the garment part around it, such as neckline versus embroidery.
- Students may overuse pocket or zipper and avoid less familiar words such as pleat, ruffle, or topstitching.
- There is and There are may need quick review when students describe one detail versus two details.
- Students may say in the front instead of on the front, or use decorative when they mean functional.

## Classroom Management Suggestions
- Keep the image keys visible on the board while students answer app-checked tasks.
- Pause before the listening task and remind students to scan image A to image D first.
- During the writing task, coach students to complete one line at a time instead of drafting a paragraph.
- Keep the speaking task short and scaffolded by letting students use the saved card as support.

## Professional Context Notes
Fashion students regularly need to notice and name small visible details in critique, sketch notes, technical conversation, and early portfolio language. This week supports that observation habit by linking detail vocabulary to practical function and visual effect.

## Cultural or Industry Notes
Some details can be both functional and decorative in fashion practice. Make room for that idea in class examples so students do not assume each feature fits only one category. Also clarify that tie in this week means a fastening detail, not a necktie accessory.

## Simplify This Week
- Use only four gallery details during the first pass: zipper, embroidery, patch pockets, and ruffle.
- Model the role language with sentence starters already visible.
- Accept short noun phrases in early practice before asking for full sentences in the writing card.

## Extend This Week
- Ask students to add one extra effect sentence with adds or makes.
- Invite students to compare two details from different gallery images.
- Ask stronger students to explain why one detail is both functional and decorative.

## Asynchronous or App-Based Adaptation
The asynchronous flow works well if the stable image keys remain visible and the app saves exact selections, matches, fill blanks, and structured lines. For teacher review, show the selected image key, the six required writing lines, the optional challenge line, the checklist, common errors, and feedback prompts. The speaking task should remain teacher-observed only with no recording or upload step.

assets.description: A single adult-learning board that shows one fashion look or sketch plus several possible inspiration-source thumbnails so students can make quick controlled source selections.
assets.notes: Keep the visible source options distinct and easy to compare on a phone screen. Avoid ambiguous or decorative thumbnails that do not support a clear controlled answer.

assets.title: Week 12 keyed inspiration-source vocabulary board A to H
assets.description: A clear adult-learning board with eight inspiration-source images labeled A to H for explicit image-to-word matching.
assets.notes: Keep the keys literal and visible. Use only source images that clearly support nature, city, street style, music, art, architecture, history, and memory. Make history a clear historical-fashion cue such as an archival illustration, vintage dress form, museum garment display, or historical silhouette board. Make memory a clear personal-memory cue such as a family photo with a fabric swatch, keepsake textile, or memory-box object, and keep both panels visibly distinct from art and architecture.

assets.title: Week 12 keyed mood-and-effect board
assets.description: A controlled four-panel board with stable visible keys and clear design cues for matching a look to one mood and one effect phrase.
assets.notes: Avoid subjective or ambiguous styling. Each panel should make the correct mood and effect obvious through visible color, silhouette, contrast, or line choices.

weeks.lesson_plan_markdown:
# Week 12: Creative Inspiration

## Overview
Week 12 moves from visible description into simple design rationale. Students learn to name common inspiration sources, connect them to visible design choices, and describe the mood or effect a design creates. The week ends with one scaffolded inspiration-note card and one short teacher-supported speaking explanation.

## Learning Objectives
- Identify common inspiration sources such as nature, city, music, art, architecture, history, memory, and movement.
- Use short rationale frames such as This design is inspired by ..., The colors come from ..., and I chose ... because ....
- Recognize simple mood and effect language such as calm, bold, playful, elegant, and modern.
- Read and listen to short inspiration notes tied to stable image keys.
- Produce one structured Design Inspiration Note Card with six required short lines.

## Professional Fashion-Design Context
Students use the kind of English they need for early concept development, inspiration-board discussion, sketch rationale, and short portfolio-ready explanation language. This week helps them move from naming visible features to explaining where a design idea comes from and why specific colors, fabrics, lines, or details were chosen.

## Language Objectives
- Name inspiration sources and simple themes.
- Connect a source to one visible design element.
- Use because to explain one design choice.
- Use The overall look is ... to describe a final impression.

## Materials Needed
- Week 12 opener board with one look and several inspiration thumbnails.
- Week 12 keyed inspiration-source board A to H.
- Week 12 keyed mood-and-effect board.
- Week 12 reusable image A to image D gallery.
- Week 12 listening clip aligned exactly to the reusable gallery.
- Optional projected or printed copies of the reusable gallery for the writing and speaking tasks.

## Suggested Sequence
1. Start with the opener so students move from detail observation to the idea of design inspiration.
2. Teach the core inspiration-source vocabulary through the keyed image board.
3. Use the mood-and-effect task to connect visible design cues to a likely impression.
4. Model short inspiration notes through reading before the listening task.
5. Use the listening task with the same stable gallery to reinforce the same source-to-design logic.
6. Consolidate the language with short phrase-practice fill blanks.
7. Move into the main structured writing card with one chosen gallery image.
8. End the online sequence with two narrow correction cards.
9. Use the teacher session for pronunciation support and one short spoken explanation.

## Timing Estimate
The student-facing weekly flow is designed for about 144 minutes total, including a 50-minute teacher-observed speaking session.

## Differentiation Options
- Keep Portuguese instructions visible while students produce English answers.
- Limit the first pass to four core inspiration sources: nature, city, music, and architecture.
- Let stronger students use the optional challenge line in the writing card.
- During the speaking task, allow students to read from the saved card before speaking more freely.

## Extension Options
- Ask students to compare two inspiration sources from the gallery using simple contrast language.
- Ask students to add one extra sentence with This creates ... or This makes the look ....
- Reuse the Week 12 gallery as a warm-up when moving into Week 13 feedback language.

## Notes for Future App Implementation
The app should keep stable visible keys on the screen whenever a task depends on them. The reusable image A to image D gallery should support the reading, listening, writing, and speaking tasks without changing key assignments. The writing card should save the chosen image key plus each required line separately. The listening task should allow replay and reveal the script only after the first completed attempt. The teacher review flow should show the selected image key, the saved structured lines, the checklist, common errors, and return-for-revision support for the writing task only.
weeks.teacher_notes_markdown:
# Teacher Notes: Week 12 - Creative Inspiration

## Common Learner Difficulties
- Students may name a visible detail but not explain where the idea comes from.
- Students may confuse source words such as reference, theme, and concept.
- Students may use inspired in instead of inspired by or write because without a full reason clause.
- Mood words can become vague unless the visual cue is strong and the answer choices are limited.

## Classroom Management Suggestions
- Keep the image keys visible on the board while students answer app-checked tasks.
- Pause before the listening task and remind students to scan image A to image D first.
- During the writing task, coach students to complete one line at a time instead of drafting a paragraph.
- Keep the speaking task short and scaffolded by letting students use the saved card as support.

## Professional Context Notes
Fashion students regularly explain where an idea comes from when discussing moodboards, sketches, concept directions, and early portfolio captions. This week supports that professional habit by linking inspiration language to specific visible choices and simple rationale.

## Cultural or Industry Notes
Reference in this week means a design reference, not a bibliographic citation. Mood should be taught as atmosphere or impression, not only personal emotion. Movement refers to visible motion or flow in the design, not only physical exercise.

## Simplify This Week
- Use only four core sources during the first pass: nature, city, music, and architecture.
- Model the rationale frames with visible sentence starters before asking students to write.
- Accept short noun phrases in early practice before asking for full because clauses in the writing card.

## Extend This Week
- Ask students to add one extra effect sentence with This creates ... or This makes the look ....
- Invite students to compare two gallery images using simple contrast language.
- Ask stronger students to explain how one source affects both color and silhouette.

## Asynchronous or App-Based Adaptation
The asynchronous flow works well if the stable image keys remain visible and the app saves exact selections, matches, fill blanks, and structured lines. For teacher review, show the selected image key, the six required writing lines, the optional challenge line, the checklist, common errors, and feedback prompts. The speaking task should remain teacher-observed only with no recording or upload step.

vocabulary_groups.title: Feedback core nouns and verbs
vocabulary_groups.description: Core words for talking about comments, revision, and improvement in a design class.

items.definition_en: Comments that help improve work.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: Comments that help make the design better.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Comentarios que ajudam a melhorar o design.
items.example_sentence_en: The student gives simple feedback on the sketch.
items.example_sentence_pt: The student gives simple feedback on the sketch.
items.professional_context_en: Feedback is the main Week 13 concept for studio critique and revision.
items.professional_context_pt: Feedback e o conceito principal da Semana 13 para critica de estudio e revisao.
items.translation_notes_pt: The borrowed word feedback is common, but students still need the full English classroom use.

items.definition_en: A short opinion or response about the work.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A short thing you say about the design.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Uma coisa curta que voce diz sobre o design.
items.example_sentence_en: My first comment is positive.
items.example_sentence_pt: My first comment is positive.
items.professional_context_en: Comment supports simple critique and response language.
items.professional_context_pt: Comment apoia a linguagem simples de critica e resposta.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to comentario.

items.definition_en: An idea for making the work better.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A polite idea for change.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Uma ideia educada para mudar algo.
items.example_sentence_en: My suggestion is to add more contrast.
items.example_sentence_pt: My suggestion is to add more contrast.
items.professional_context_en: Suggestion is key for polite critique before revision.
items.professional_context_pt: Suggestion e importante para a critica educada antes da revisao.
items.translation_notes_pt: Teach as polite advice, not as an order.

items.definition_en: A change made after feedback.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A change you make after comments.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Uma mudanca que voce faz depois dos comentarios.
items.example_sentence_en: The revision makes the caption clearer.
items.example_sentence_pt: The revision makes the caption clearer.
items.professional_context_en: Revision connects critique language to the next design step.
items.professional_context_pt: Revision conecta a linguagem de critica ao proximo passo do design.
items.translation_notes_pt: Revision here means change after feedback, not only checking again.

items.definition_en: A strong positive feature of the work.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: The best good part of the design.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: A melhor parte positiva do design.
items.example_sentence_en: The main strength is the silhouette.
items.example_sentence_pt: The main strength is the silhouette.
items.professional_context_en: Strength helps students move beyond very general praise.
items.professional_context_pt: Strength ajuda os alunos a irem alem de elogios muito gerais.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to ponto forte.

vocabulary_groups.title: Positive comment and reason frames
vocabulary_groups.description: High-frequency feedback phrases for saying what works and why.

items.definition_en: A simple way to start a positive comment.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A simple beginning for saying something good.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Um comeco simples para dizer algo bom.
items.example_sentence_en: I like the color palette.
items.example_sentence_pt: I like the color palette.
items.professional_context_en: I like ... is a safe A2 frame for beginner critique.
items.professional_context_pt: I like ... e uma estrutura segura de nivel A2 para critica inicial.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to eu gosto de.

items.definition_en: Is successful or looks effective.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: Looks good and makes sense in the design.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Fica bom e faz sentido no design.
items.example_sentence_en: The fabric works well with the long dress.
items.example_sentence_pt: The fabric works well with the long dress.
items.professional_context_en: Works well is useful for palette, silhouette, fabric, and detail comments.
items.professional_context_pt: Works well e util para comentarios sobre paleta, silhueta, tecido e detalhe.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to funciona bem.

items.definition_en: The best or most successful part of the design.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: The part that works best.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: A parte que funciona melhor.
items.example_sentence_en: The strongest part is the jacket shape.
items.example_sentence_pt: The strongest part is the jacket shape.
items.professional_context_en: This frame helps students name one specific strength in critique.
items.professional_context_pt: Essa estrutura ajuda os alunos a nomear um ponto forte especifico na critica.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to a parte mais forte.

items.definition_en: A word used to give a reason.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A word for saying why.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Uma palavra para dizer por que.
items.example_sentence_en: I like the look because it is balanced.
items.example_sentence_pt: I like the look because it is balanced.
items.professional_context_en: Because is the key Week 13 connector for useful feedback.
items.professional_context_pt: Because e o principal conector da Semana 13 para um feedback util.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to porque.

items.definition_en: A phrase used to explain a design effect.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A way to say what effect the design makes.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Uma forma de dizer qual efeito o design cria.
items.example_sentence_en: This creates a calm mood.
items.example_sentence_pt: This creates a calm mood.
items.professional_context_en: This creates helps students explain visual effect without long writing.
items.professional_context_pt: This creates ajuda os alunos a explicar efeito visual sem escrita longa.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to isso cria.

vocabulary_groups.title: Suggestion and polite critique
vocabulary_groups.description: Frames and verbs for making one respectful improvement idea.

items.definition_en: A polite way to give a suggestion.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A polite way to say one idea for change.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Uma forma educada de dizer uma ideia de mudanca.
items.example_sentence_en: You could add more contrast.
items.example_sentence_pt: You could add more contrast.
items.professional_context_en: You could is the main suggestion frame for Week 13.
items.professional_context_pt: You could e a principal estrutura de sugestao da Semana 13.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to voce poderia.
items.pronunciation_notes: Stress COULD in short polite speech.

items.definition_en: A softer and more careful suggestion frame.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: A softer way to give advice.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Uma forma mais suave de dar um conselho.
items.example_sentence_en: Maybe you could simplify the caption.
items.example_sentence_pt: Maybe you could simplify the caption.
items.professional_context_en: Maybe you could helps students sound respectful in critique.
items.professional_context_pt: Maybe you could ajuda os alunos a soar respeitosos na critica.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to talvez voce pudesse or talvez voce poderia.

items.definition_en: To put something new into the design or text.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: To put one more thing in.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Colocar mais uma coisa.
items.example_sentence_en: Add one small detail near the neckline.
items.example_sentence_pt: Add one small detail near the neckline.
items.professional_context_en: Add supports practical critique of detail, contrast, and information.
items.professional_context_pt: Add apoia a critica pratica de detalhe, contraste e informacao.
items.translation_notes_pt: Bridge to acrescentar or adicionar.

items.definition_en: To make something different.
items.learner_friendly_definition_en: To make it different from now.
items.learner_friendly_definition_pt: Fazer algo ficar diferente do que esta agora.
items.example_sentence_en: Change the color balance a little.
items.example_sentence_pt: Change the color balance a little.

weeks.lesson_plan_markdown:
# Week 13: Giving Simple Design Feedback

## Overview
Week 13 helps students move from describing and explaining a design to responding to someone else's work. Students learn how to say what works well, explain why, give one polite suggestion, and state one revision step in simple English.

The main written artifact stays A2-first. Students do not write a paragraph and do not work toward a word-count target. Instead, they complete a scaffolded Design Feedback Note + Revision Plan Card with 6 required sentence-frame lines and 1 optional challenge line. Line 6 uses one stable pattern: `This will make the design more ___.` The optional challenge line is not required for completion and should be saved separately only if the student chooses to complete it. This keeps the writing concrete, teacher-reviewable, and aligned with the Module 1 guardrails while still preparing students for Week 14.

## Learning Objectives
- Recognize and use core feedback words such as `feedback`, `comment`, `suggestion`, `revision`, and `strength`.
- Match reusable English feedback phrases to Portuguese support and to their feedback function.
- Distinguish between a positive comment, a reason, a suggestion, and a revision plan.
- Read four short feedback comments and match them to the correct image key.
- Listen to four numbered spoken feedback comments and identify the correct image, strength, or suggestion.
- Complete sentence frames with `because`, `could`, and revision verbs.
- Complete a scaffolded Design Feedback Note + Revision Plan Card with 6 required lines and 1 optional challenge line.
- Give one short positive comment and one short suggestion aloud during the teacher session.

## Professional Fashion-Design Context
Week 13 connects English to beginner studio critique, sketch review, caption revision, and peer response. Students are not doing advanced design criticism. They are learning how to respond to a look, sketch, or mini board in a respectful, useful, and beginner-friendly way.

This week also prepares students for the Week 14 mini design board. The feedback structure matters professionally: identify one strength, explain why it works, suggest one improvement, and say one next revision step.

## Language Objectives
- Use positive feedback frames such as `I like the ...`, `The strongest part is ...`, and `This works well`.
- Use reason language with `because`, `This creates ...`, and `This makes ...`.
- Use polite suggestion frames such as `You could ...`, `Maybe you could ...`, and `Try using ...`.
- Use revision language such as `I will revise ...`, `I will add ...`, `I will change ...`, `clarify`, and `simplify`.
- Use design focus words such as `color palette`, `silhouette`, `detail`, `fabric`, `contrast`, `balanced`, and `clear`.

## Materials Needed
- One Week 13 opener design board with one clear adult-oriented fashion look or sketch.
- One reusable Week 13 gallery labeled only `image A`, `image B`, `image C`, and `image D`.
- One Week 13 listening clip aligned exactly to the reusable gallery.
- Visible sentence frames for positive comment, reason, suggestion, and revision-plan language.
- Student writing space for the Design Feedback Note + Revision Plan Card.
- Optional classroom support: printed gallery cards, projected gallery view, or teacher-selected critique examples.

## Suggested Sequence
1. `m01w13-a01` Welcome Back: students look at one feedback-ready image and answer five short visible-clue questions about what works well.
2. `m01w13-a02` Feedback Phrase Bank: students complete the main phrase matching set and short phrase-function support matches.
3. `m01w13-a03` Positive, Reason, Suggestion, or Revision Plan?: students classify eight short feedback sentence cards.
4. `m01w13-a04` Read: students use the `image A` to `image D` gallery, read four short feedback comments, and answer image-match and detail questions.
5. `m01w13-a05` Listen: students use the same gallery, listen to one numbered audio clip, and answer image and suggestion questions that match the script exactly.
6. `m01w13-a06` Build Better Feedback: students complete six feedback frames with `because`, `could`, and revision language.
7. `m01w13-a07` Design Feedback Note + Revision Plan Card: students choose one gallery image and complete a teacher-reviewed structured writing card with 6 required lines plus 1 optional challenge line saved separately only if completed.
8. `m01w13-a08` Review and Improve: students correct two short Week 13 feedback sentences and save the improved versions.
9. `m01w13-a09` Teacher Session: students practice pronunciation and give one short mini critique using the selected image and saved card from `m01w13-a07` as read-only support.

## Timing Estimate
- `m01w13-a01` 7 minutes
- `m01w13-a02` 14 minutes
- `m01w13-a03` 12 minutes
- `m01w13-a04` 14 minutes
- `m01w13-a05` 12 minutes
- `m01w13-a06` 9 minutes
- `m01w13-a07` 18 minutes
- `m01w13-a08` 7 minutes
- `m01w13-a09` 50 minutes

Total planned time: 143 minutes.

The asynchronous or app-style portion is 93 minutes. The teacher-led speaking session is 50 minutes.

## Differentiation Options
- Keep Portuguese instructions visible while students produce English answers.
- Keep the reusable image A to image D gallery visible during reading, listening, writing, and speaking tasks.
- Limit the first pass to four core feedback frames: `I like ...`, `because`, `You could ...`, and `I will revise ...`.
- Let students choose the simplest gallery image for the writing card if they need a clearer critique target.
- During the speaking task, allow students to read from the saved feedback card before speaking more freely.

## Extension Options
- Ask stronger learners to use the optional challenge line with `Maybe you could ... because ...`.
- Ask stronger learners to add one extra sentence using `This creates ...` or `This makes the look ...`.
- Reuse the Week 13 gallery as a feedback warm-up before students start Week 14 mini design board revision.

## Notes for Future App Implementation
Week 13 should preserve one stable interaction flow from recognition to production:

- one opener image board for a fast visible-clue critique review
- one main phrase-matching task where matching remains the primary saved output
- one single-choice classification task with student-facing category labels only
- one reading task using a fixed visible-key strategy `image A` to `image D`
- one listening task whose numbered audio script matches the same `image A` to `image D` gallery and answer key exactly
- one fill-blank language task where the primary saved output stays sentence completion
- one teacher-reviewed structured writing card with separate required line fields plus one optional line saved separately instead of a paragraph box
- one sentence-correction task with explicit accepted answers
- one teacher-observed speaking checkpoint that shows the previously selected image and saved writing card from `m01w13-a07` as read-only support and does not record audio

The reusable gallery should stay consistent across reading, listening, writing, and speaking so students do not need a new image set when they move into the main written and spoken artifacts.
weeks.teacher_notes_markdown:
# Teacher Notes: Week 13 - Giving Simple Design Feedback

## Common Learner Difficulties
Students may know design vocabulary from earlier weeks but still give vague feedback such as `good` or `nice` without naming a real feature. Some learners may confuse a positive comment with a suggestion, or write `because` without a full reason clause. Students may also use `can` instead of `could` for polite critique, mix details from more than one gallery image, or turn the writing card into a short paragraph instead of six separate lines.

## Classroom Management Suggestions
Keep the reusable `image A` to `image D` gallery visible throughout the week. Students should be able to point to the same image during reading, listening, writing, and speaking tasks. Move steadily from recognition to production: opener, phrase bank, sentence classification, reading, listening, fill blanks, structured writing, correction, then speaking. During the writing task, remind students to complete one line at a time instead of drafting freely.

## Professional Context Notes
Fashion students regularly need to respond to sketches, captions, and early design ideas in critique sessions. This week gives them a beginner-friendly way to do that in English. The goal is not advanced criticism. The goal is useful studio language that can name one strength, explain one reason, offer one respectful suggestion, and state one revision step before the final mini design board.

## Cultural or Industry Notes
Explain that feedback in design class should be useful and respectful, not only positive or only negative. `Suggestion` should be taught as polite advice, not a command. `Revision` means a change made after feedback, not just a general review. Also note that borrowed words such as `feedback` may feel familiar to learners, but the full English critique phrases still need practice.

## Simplify This Week
- Keep the main feedback structure visible at all times: positive comment, reason, suggestion, revision plan.
- Accept short design-focused answers before asking for complete longer lines in the writing card.
- Use only the clearest gallery image first for students who need more support.
- Keep the writing card at exactly six required lines:
  - `I like the ___.`
  - `It works well because ___.`
  - `The strongest part is ___.`
  - `You could ___.`
  - `I will revise ___.`
  - `This will make the design more ___.`
- Use the optional challenge line only if the student is ready:
  - `Maybe you could ___ because ___.`
  The optional challenge line is not required for completion. Save and show it separately only if the student completes it.

## Extend This Week
- Ask stronger learners to add one extra effect sentence with `This creates ...` or `This makes the look ...`.
- Invite stronger learners to compare two gallery images and explain which one receives stronger feedback.
- In the teacher session, ask one follow-up question such as `Why does that detail work well?` or `What will you revise first?`

## Asynchronous or App-Based Adaptation
The opener, phrase bank, sentence-classification task, reading task, listening task, fill-blank task, and correction task can all be app-checked with immediate feedback if the answer data stays explicit. The Design Feedback Note + Revision Plan Card should remain teacher-visible because it is the main written artifact, uses six required lines plus one optional challenge line, and benefits from one revision cycle. The optional line should appear separately in teacher review only if the student completed it, and the required task should not be marked incomplete when that optional line is blank. The speaking checkpoint should remain teacher-observed and non-recorded, with the app serving only to display the selected gallery image from `m01w13-a07`, the saved card, the speaking frames, and completion notes.

assets.title: Week 14 model mini design board
assets.description: A model mini design board with visible student-friendly section labels and short readable text aligned to the Week 14 reading and listening tasks.
assets.notes: Keep the section labels and text readable on a phone screen. The model board must visibly support opener answers and align exactly with the reading text and the listening script.

assets.title: Week 14 cumulative review board
assets.description: A keyed cumulative review board for garment, part, fabric, detail, and inspiration review with visible clues that support app-checked matching.
assets.notes: Keep all visual clues visible and stable. The board should support literal key matching and simple category recognition without hidden logic.

assets.title: Week 14 reusable four-panel gallery image A to image D
assets.description: A reusable four-panel gallery labeled only image A, image B, image C, and image D for label matching, structured drafting, final submission, and the teacher presentation session.
assets.notes: Keep the literal image A to image D labels visible and stable. Each panel should show one distinct adult-oriented fashion look with clear garment, fabric, detail, and inspiration cues so the selected image key can be reused meaningfully.

assets.title: Week 14 model mini-board presentation
